title: Common App for international students: a complete timeline
summary: A month-by-month plan for the Common App, from building a college list to the enrollment reply date, with the points international applicants most often miss.

body:
## In short

- The Common App is a single online application used by many US colleges. You fill in one profile and send it to each college you choose.
- Each college sets its own deadlines, test policies, supplements and document rules. The Common App form is only one part of the application.
- The cycle opens in the summer before you start. Early and regular deadlines fall in the autumn and early winter of the year you apply.
- International applicants should also plan for transcript translation, English test results, and the fee waiver process, which the Common App explains on its official site.

## What the Common App does and does not do

The Common App collects your personal information, activities, family details, school information and essays, then sends them to the colleges you select. It does not decide admission. Some colleges use their own application instead, and some ask for extra supplements.

Use the Common App requirement grid for each college on your list. The grid shows which forms, essays and documents each college asks for and which deadlines apply. The official grid is a PDF published by the Common App, and it is the authority for each college's requirements.

## Step 1: Build your college list

Choose a range of colleges, some where your profile is strong, some where it is typical and some where it is a reach. Check each college's international admission page, its English test policy, whether it accepts your school certificate, and whether it offers financial aid for international students. Do not rely on rankings alone.

## Step 2: Create your account and profile

Create an account on the Common App site, then fill in your personal information, family information, school information, activities, honours and testing. Use your passport name exactly. Keep your school records to hand, because the school section may ask for dates and grades.

The form has fields for several English tests and for standardised tests where a college asks for them. Enter results only from official score reports, and check which tests each college accepts.

## Step 3: Fee waivers

The Common App's own guidance defines a fee waiver as a request to the college to remove the application fee. A Common App fee waiver must be confirmed by your school counsellor, and colleges can also run their own fee waiver policy. Check each college's policy, because some accept Common App waivers and some do not.

If you are an international applicant with limited means, ask your school counsellor early and check each college's international fee rules.

## Step 4: Essays and activities

The Common App includes a personal essay, which is the main writing task, and a list of activities. Read the essay prompts for the cycle you are applying in, and check whether any college on your list asks for a supplement. Write a first draft early, then revise it with a teacher or counsellor. Keep the activities list specific, with hours, dates and roles.

## Step 5: Transcripts and recommendation letters

Ask your school to send transcripts directly, and check whether the college needs an official translation. Ask your teachers for recommendation letters early, and give them a list of the colleges and deadlines. Many colleges need a counsellor report as well. Check the requirement grid for each college.

## Step 6: Test scores

Some colleges require test scores, some accept them as optional, and some do not consider them at all. Check the policy for each college. If a college accepts English test results, use the official score report route that the college names.

## A timeline for the applicant

**Spring, the year before entry.** Shortlist colleges, check international policies and begin drafting essays.

**Summer.** Create the Common App account when the cycle opens, complete the profile, and draft your essays.

**Autumn.** Finish essays, request recommendation letters, send transcripts and complete any test requirements. Submit early applications by the early deadline if you plan to apply early.

**Early winter.** Submit regular applications by the regular deadlines. Check that every document has arrived at each college.

**Spring.** Expect decisions, compare financial aid offers and check your visa and housing plans.

**Early May.** Make your enrollment decision and submit the deposit by the reply date that the college sets.

Confirm each date on the official Common App site and on each college's page. Dates change every cycle, and some colleges set their own deadlines.

## Common mistakes

- Missing a college's own deadline while focusing on the Common App date.
- Sending a practice score instead of an official report.
- Leaving out a translation or an official copy of a school certificate.
- Ignoring a supplement that appears only after a college is added.
- Forgetting the financial aid form that some colleges require for international students.

## Common mistakes with international documents

International applicants often lose time at the document stage. School records may need to be sent directly by the school, in a sealed envelope or through an official electronic route. Translations may need to be certified by a recognised translator, and some colleges want a grade conversion explained by the school. Ask your school counsellor to explain how your grades will be read by a US college, because a grading scale that looks high in one country can look different in another.

## Interviews and supplements

Some colleges offer optional alumni interviews, and some ask every applicant to complete a supplement. An interview is a conversation, not an exam. Prepare two or three specific reasons you chose the college, and practise talking about your school and your projects in English. Supplements are often short, but they can carry a deadline of their own, so put them on your tracker as soon as they appear.

## Financial aid and the financial form

Many US colleges that offer need-based aid to international students ask for an additional financial form. Read each college's international aid page, and note whether the aid is need-blind for international applicants or whether it is limited. Do not assume that a college with a high ranking has the same aid policy as a college with a lower ranking. Ask the financial aid office for the deadline and the documents they require, including tax or income evidence from your home country where asked.

## Managing many deadlines

A simple tracker helps. Make one row for each college, with columns for the Common App deadline, the college's own deadline, the test requirement, the supplement, the recommendation letters, the transcript and the financial aid form. Update the tracker each week, and check your student account for confirmation that each document has been received.

## Your visa and the next step

If you are admitted, start the visa process early. A student visa for the United States requires an approved form and an interview at a US embassy or consulate, and appointment availability can be limited in some countries. Ask the college for the form it issues to international students, and plan the visa interview as soon as you have the form. Consult the official US visa information site for the current steps.

## Checklist

- [ ] Check the Common App requirement grid for every college on your list.
- [ ] Create your account and complete the profile with passport details.
- [ ] Confirm each college's English and standardised test policy.
- [ ] Ask your counsellor about a fee waiver if you need one.
- [ ] Draft the personal essay and any supplements early.
- [ ] Request recommendation letters and transcripts with time to spare.
- [ ] Track every college deadline and confirmation of receipt.
- [ ] Confirm the enrollment reply date for each offer you receive.
